144-P41-DW
Management: Neurological Conditions
2 sections
  • 00001
  • Jin Woo Hong
  • In this course, students will learn to provide rehabilitation services to clients of all ages who are affected by common neurological conditions. Students will explore cases involving clientele at various levels of complexity, and in a variety of settings therefore requiring various levels of analysis and responsibility for the profession. Familiar conditions that will be covered in greater depth are stroke and Parkinson’s disease. New conditions will include multiple sclerosis, traumatic brain injury, cerebral palsy, spinal cord injury, and other neurological conditions. During lab sessions, students will further develop skills in performing tasks to collect evaluative data and provide treatment interventions, including hands-on skills, following established protocols and using technology and assistive devices. Teaching approaches will include case-based learning, collaborative and group work as well as individual and group preparatory activities.

This hands-on course fosters creativity, adaptability, and practical skills in health promotion.

350-0B2-DW
Forensic Psychology
2 sections
  • 00001
  • Caroline Chochol
  • Forensic psychology focuses on the observation and application of psychological principles within legal and criminal justice contexts. Students will explore key areas such as criminal behaviour analysis, mental health assessments, eyewitness testimony, and the psychology of law enforcement. A distinctive feature of this course is the hands-on observational component, where students will engage in structured observations of real or simulated cases to develop skills in behavioural analysis and critical evaluation.

350-0B3-DW
Social Psychology
2 sections
  • 00001
  • Nadia Vracotas
  • Social psychology is the scientific study of how an individual’s mental processes and behaviour are affected by the perceived or imagined presence and influence of other people. We will examine how people think about and interpret the behaviour of others, and what attracts people to one another. We will talk about attributions, attitudes, stereotypes, prejudice, and cognitive dissonance. Subtle and not-so-subtle forms of peer pressure will be discussed and demonstrated, including conformity, compliance, persuasion, and obedience. Students will carry out structured observations to demonstrate how theories learned in class are applied in real-life contexts.
  • Psychology

350-FWS-DW
Complémentaire en Psychologie - Ensemble I
2 sections
  • Derrière le voile : Psychologie des théories du complot
  • 60001
  • Stephane Gaskin
  • Les théories du complot sont des explications d’événements importants fondées sur des intrigues secrètes de groupes puissants et malveillants. Ce cours permet aux étudiants d’examiner comment ces théories se développent et circulent dans la société, selon une perspective psychologique. Les caractéristiques de personnalité associées à la croyance aux théories du complot seront analysées, de même que les besoins et motivations psychologiques qui facilitent leur adhésion. Les étudiants analyseront les mécanismes menant à la méfiance envers les sources officielles d’information, ainsi que les raisons pour lesquelles ces théories séduisent. Les effets néfastes de ces croyances — préjugés, rejet de la science, violence, radicalisation — seront aussi explorés. Par des lectures et des exercices en classe, les étudiants développeront leur pensée critique pour reconnaître et comprendre ces discours.
  • This course is taught in French only.
  • Friday, February 13, 2026
  • Wednesday, April 8, 2026
  • Tuesday11:30 AM - 2:30 PM3E.9Class

360-124-DW
Principles of Mathematics and Logic
1 section
  • 00001
  • Sarah Allen
  • This course introduces students to the nature of formal reasoning and central methods and concepts in logic and mathematics. Topics covered may include: the nature of philosophical arguments, deductive vs. inductive reasoning, the languages of propositional and predicate logic, forms of logical proof, the axiomatic method in mathematics, and Euclidean and non-Euclidean geometry. The course will also explore the relationship between logic and critical thinking, the distinction between logic and psychology, and the distinction between logic and rhetoric. Throughout the course, we will see the significance of formal reasoning for the liberal arts and its crucial role in understanding both the world and ourselves.

  • Brian Mader

Due to the extensive planning required for this course, interested students must apply by the end of the second term of the preceding academic year.

  • Particle Physics, Building and Using Detectors
  • 00006
  • Manuel Toharia Zapata
  • Particle physics is generally thought of as just a fundamental research science. However, it has a growing presence in our daily lives, notably in cutting-edge medical treatments. Also, radioactivity from natural sources as well as from man-made sources must be carefully measured and controlled (radon gas in basements, cosmic radiation, radioactive waste, etc.). In this course, students will be provided with the tools to build and understand a simple and safe particle detector and then use it to study various different possible topics, such as building a smoke detector, studying the Bragg peak of alpha particles in air, performing alpha particle spectrometry, or measuring and studying the flux of cosmic rays on the ground.

  • Dawson Aqua Research Team
  • 00007
  • Adamo Petosa
  • “Water, water everywhere, but not a drop to drink.” While 71% of Earth’s surface is covered in water (earning our planet the nickname Blue Planet), only about 3% of this water is freshwater. More than 99% of freshwater is not readily accessible for consumption, with only 0.3% of Earth’s freshwater found in lakes, rivers and wetlands. Water, for which animals migrate and humans staring at the heavens have danced, is threatened. Join the Dawson Aqua Research Team (DART), led by Geology, as we call upon knowledge from multiple scientific disciplines to work on protecting and restoring our water resources. Pilot studies will enable us to seek out solutions to a multitude of challenges facing aquatic environments and their inhabitants. Students will have the opportunity to design and construct a laboratory-scale project that addresses and/or counteracts one of Earth’s current water-related challenges. Water is at the crossroads. Join us in protecting this essential, life-giving resource!

142-421-DW
Applied Dosimetry
1 section
  • 00001
  • Piotr Pater, Radiation Oncology team McGill, Russell Ruo, William Parker
  • This Applied Dosimetry course deals with radiation dosimetry and concentrates on beam measurement techniques, quality assurance issues in treatment planning, as well as the special techniques used in treatment planning and delivery. The basic quantities and units used in dosimetry are discussed in detail and their application in the calculation of clinical dose distributions is explained. The course starts with a discussion of single photon beams and progresses through dose distributions obtained with multiple photon beams to electron beams and dosimetry in brachytherapy. Students will produce and evaluate clinical treatment plans.

370-215-DW
Religion and Popular Culture
1 section
  • 00001
  • Amanda Rosini
  • Because popular culture both reflects and affects the society in which it is situated, it contains many references to the religions practiced within that society. These references can be explicit or implicit, conscious or unconscious. In this course we will focus on a number of particular cultural objects containing these references, examining the religious components inherent in the objects and analyzing the way in which their meanings have or have not changed with the transition from religious to secular context. This can help us analyze some of the transformations occurring within our society even as we live through those changes. In addition to examining some of these objects together as a class, students will choose an individual object to analyze and will present their findings in writing as well as sharing these with the rest of the class in an oral presentation.

370-917-DW
Cults and Culture
2 sections
  • 00001
  • Laurel Missen Andrew
  • The course explores the origins, beliefs, rituals and social organizations of some of the new religious movements that contribute to the religious landscape of North America. Sociological, historical and psychological approaches will be employed in the study. Among other subjects, the course will discuss theories of conversion, the “brainwashing”/deprogramming controversy, charismatic authority and the ritual processes within these sects. The contentious status of Scientology, the Wiccan and the Raelian traditions will be analyzed, as will their relationships to their host societies. This course represents a scientific and academic study of New Religious Movements and as such maintains a safe and structured environment for students.

370-A02-DW
Religion, Spirituality, and Psychology
1 section
  • 00001
  • Philip Lagace
  • This course will examine the contributions of classical theorists in the psychology of religion (e.g., William James, Sigmund Freud, Carl Jung, Gordon Allport, Erich Fromm, Erik Erikson, and Abraham Maslow). The second part of the course will consist of applying selected psychological theories to various religious phenomena. It will provide a consideration of some of the theories and hypotheses that guide contemporary empirical research. Sample topics to be covered include the theories of religious conversion and possession states; motives for participating in religious communities and religious rituals; intrinsic, extrinsic and quest religious orientations; the relationship between God-image and self-image; religious orientation and attachment style (secure, anxious and avoidant); the spiritual quest as a transformation of the grieving process; the neurophysiology of mystical experiences; and the psychology of sects and cults.

370-A03-DW
Tech Gods
1 section
  • 00001
  • Calogero Miceli
  • This course examines the ways in which technology, media, religions, and social groups intersect. In addition to exploring the religious qualities of brands and digital media, we study how established religious individuals and groups have adapted their faith and practices to the ever-changing technological landscape. While a few groups have been protectionist and rejected such advancements (calling instead for more traditional or orthodox means of understanding or practicing their faiths), we find that many more have embraced modern technology in varying ways. Some, utilizing web searches, social media, and online platforms, have been able to reach beyond their local congregations to globalize and promote religious ideas and figures. Yet others have used these same tools to wreak havoc on the world by recruiting, promoting, organizing, and executing deadly terrorist attacks. The course aims to comprehend the impact and potential that technology provides to religions across the globe.

370-BXS-03
Social science: applications in religion studies
1 section
  • Jesus: He's Everywhere
  • 00001
  • Calogero Miceli
  • Who was Jesus? Was he married? Did he kill? The following course explores the figure of Jesus throughout the centuries from historical and literary sources to modern depictions of Jesus in popular culture such as film, art, comics, and more. Students survey some of the primary sources associated with the historical Jesus such as the traditional Christian canonical gospels of the New Testament. Along with these we explore the Jesus found in apocryphal Christian literature, ancient documents which detail interesting, often lesser-known accounts of Jesus as a child and miracle worker. The course teaches students to think critically about a major figure of our time using various social scientific approaches. In this course, we investigate and critique various understandings of who Jesus was and how he is understood and perceived today.

300-0B2-DW
Solidarity in Action: A Local Perspective
1 section
  • 00001
  • Benjamin Lander
  • This field research and experiential learning geography course offers students the opportunity to conduct fieldwork in Montreal about a local social justice issue; this year’s theme is migrant justice. Over the course of this intensive, students will engage in a series of hands-on workshops, activities, and conversations with people directly impacted by injustice and organizations working to make change across Montreal. In collaboration with over a dozen community partners, this course emphasizes learning from people with lived experience and learning alongside social movements, and the use of field research methodology. Through reflective journals, collaborative projects, and participation in conferences, students will gain research experience while deepening their understanding of how the immigration system impacts communities and various approaches to social change.

Introduction to Social Science Research
14 sections
  • 00001
  • Marc-André Girouard
  • Introduction to Social Science Research (IR) is the first of the four methodology courses and is normally taken in the student’s first term of the program. The goal of the course is to develop and apply appropriate work methods to the social science disciplines. Students learn and practice skills such as accessing and organizing relevant information, using appropriate technologies, identifying academic and non-academic sources, evaluating the reliability of the sources, summarizing an author’s main idea, citing sources, building a bibliography, communicating their ideas orally and in writing, and effectively working in a group. This course establishes a practical foundation for successful and ethical work in the social sciences and is the pre-requisite for the two methodology courses that follow: Qualitative Methods and Quantitative Analysis.

  • 00011
  • Alyssa Scirocco
  • Recently, growing interest has emerged in how beliefs, attitudes and cognitive framing shape human behaviour and outcomes. From growth versus fixed mindsets in education, to resilience in the face of trauma, to the role of mindset in mental health, athletic performance, leadership, and economic mobility, the influence of mindset appears across many domains of social life. Debates continue over how much and in what ways mindset can truly shape human experiences. Over the course of the semester, you will complete a research paper that draws on peer-reviewed research examining mindset from three social science disciplines. The theme of this course is intentionally broad, allowing you to explore how mindset operates in an area that genuinely interests you. The aim of the course is for you to develop a well-reasoned, evidence-based argument that thoughtfully engages with existing research and contributes to ongoing conversations about the role mindset plays in shaping human experience.

  • Peace and Social Order
  • 00012
  • Ivan Freud
  • In this IS class, each student will be asked to select a contemporary crisis related to the degradation of our physical environment, moments or movements of social disorder, or any of our on-going wars. The chosen aspect will then be looked at from three different perspectives; the historical background so as to contextualize the event, an understanding the economic causes of the event, and finally, the effects on individuals through psychology or on groups through sociology. Students will thus learn to identify both the potential causes and effects of violent and non-violent responses to conflict thereby developing not only a greater global awareness but also a greater self-awareness in terms of one’s personal relationship with the issue at hand. Finally, in the conclusion, students will summarize the conclusions drawn from their three main aspects, consider the potential aftermaths of various proposed solutions, and present their own viable solution to the issue.

  • The Social Impact of AI
  • 00015
  • Michel Fournier-Simard
  • One of the most crucial issues of our time for social scientists is to understand how Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming democratic societies. In this integrative seminar, students are asked to produce a paper on an AI topic, integrating the perspective from three Social Science disciplines. Students will be introduced to a series of important social impacts of AI themes such as AI Ethics, Bias, Privacy, and Regulation. In the past, students have produced papers on topics such as emotional intelligence, AI in Healthcare, police biases, AI in the military, facial recognition, the regulation of GAFAM, digital democracy, and much more. You can find more information on this class here: https://www.dawsoncollege.qc.ca/ai/portfolios/algorithmic-policing/

  • The Integrative Seminar is the last of the four methodology courses and is home to the Comprehensive Examination. This course provides students an opportunity to synthesize their knowledge acquired in the Social Science program. The student will reflect on the learning and growth acquired during the program, investigate a significant issue, question a problem related to the seminar theme using at least three Social Science disciplines, communicate their findings through an oral presentation, and finally produce an evidence-based paper or a project. Purposeful integration will address the linkages and differences among social sciences and show how their combined use makes for a deeper understanding of the selected issue.

  • Sports, Culture, and Media
  • 00017
  • Jamilah Dei-sharpe, Marian Misdrahi Flores
  • Sports are a global phenomenon that transcends national boundaries, bringing communities together and fostering social bonds. Viewed through a social sciences lens, they reveal how societal norms, values, identities, and the political and economic structures are expressed and reinforced. Likewise, the study of cultural phenomena offers insight into the diverse religious expressions, customs, and belief systems that inform how societies live, interact, and evolve. Lastly, the media plays a central role in shaping public perception. The rise of the Internet and social networks has transformed how individuals communicate, access information, and engage with the world. As part of this course, students will apply knowledge from the Social Science disciplines to produce a comprehensive essay on a topic related to sports, culture, or media. The essay must integrate three disciplinary perspectives, demonstrating critical thinking and interdisciplinary understanding.

  • Controversial Issues
  • 00021
  • Evelyne Marcil
  • In this final methods course, our theme is “Controversial Issues,” and these last few years have been full of them: racism, Roe vs. Wade, mental health, addiction, cancel culture, global warming, social media, cryptocurrencies, the role of AI in education—and even micro-dosing psychedelics for happiness. The list seems endless. Over the course of the semester, you will complete a research paper, drawing on peer-reviewed research from three social science disciplines, which takes a position on a debate within the field. The theme of this course is deliberately broad to allow students to focus on an issue that interests them; I leave it to each student to define “issue” and apply the theme to whatever most intrigues them. The principal aim of the course is for you to develop a well-reasoned and well-researched argument on your topic.

  • Power, Social Control, and the Individual
  • 00023
  • Ray Claudio Pino
  • In this course, you will engage in a research project that examines a contemporary global or national issue related to the themes of power and social control, along with their implications for society and the individual. You have the freedom to choose a topic that sparks your interest, provided it is formally approved by your instructor. Consider exploring subjects such as current wars or conflicts; the military-industrial complex; Orwellian surveillance systems; AI and transhumanism; the impact of mass media and the manufacturing of consent; or addictions to social networking, gambling, or substance dependency. You will produce a comprehensive academic research paper based on primary and secondary sources drawn from three different social science disciplines. This process will enable you to uncover the origins, causes, and consequences of your chosen topic, as well as potential solutions, fostering a deeper understanding of the complexities of social order in our world today.

Quantitative Analysis
21 sections
  • 00001
  • Gemma Albanese
  • Quantitative Analysis (QA) is one of four methodology courses and is taken in either the student’s third or fourth term. The goal of the course is to interpret human realities by using quantitative analysis in the Social Sciences. Students will learn to recognize quantitative analysis, to formulate an operational hypothesis, describe quantitative data collections, to process data using descriptive and inferential measures, to describe the relationships between variables, and apply critical thinking to the interpretation of quantitative analysis. Students will also learn the importance of maintaining ethical standards in data collection and interpretation.

300-QAF-DW
Méthodes Quantitatives pour Commerce
1 section
  • 60001
  • Michel Mayer
  • Suivi en troisième année par les étudiant·es du profil « Commerce », ce cours est l’un des quatre cours de méthodologie obligatoires. Il permettra aux étudiant·es de se familiariser avec l'analyse quantitative en sciences humaines afin d’interpréter les réalités humaines à l'aide de données numériques. Basé sur une approche scientifique, ce cours permettra de recourir aux statistiques descriptives et inférentielles pour mieux comprendre la société. Parmi les notions du cours figurent l’exploration, le résumé, la représentation et l’analyse des données. Les étudiant·es estimeront les paramètres d'une population à partir d’échantillons statistiques et testeront leurs hypothèses. Ils·elles apprendront à utiliser Excel pour organiser des données, présenter des résultats et effectuer des analyses statistiques. Le cours préparera les étudiant·es à l'étude des méthodes quantitatives au niveau universitaire et à l'analyse statistique dans le domaine des affaires et de la recherche sociale.

300-TH1-DW
Thematic Issues
4 sections
  • 00001
  • Daniel Ruiz-Serna
  • Teachers will lead students through an examination of a contemporary issue from the perspective of at least three different social science disciplines. Students will contextualize the issue in place and time, as well as differentiate the theoretical approaches of the disciplines used. Students will make use of acquired competencies from the three different Social Sciences disciplines to help them generate potential research questions emanating from the analysis of an issue that will be provided by their teacher.

Social Service

388-2A2-DW
Professional Communication and Relationship Skills II
1 section
  • 00002
  • Rosemary Barrett
  • This 75-hour advanced course builds upon the foundational skills acquired in Professional Communication and Relationship Skills I, offering students in the Social Service program an in-depth exploration of essential interpersonal competencies and effective interviewing techniques required for successful engagement in the field with different client populations. Participants will further develop their abilities to communicate effectively with a diverse client population, build strong professional relationships, and navigate challenging interpersonal dynamics within the context of social service settings while considering ethical considerations. Students will explore personal and professional values and identify, describe, and process value conflicts and ethical dilemmas based on case examples from the field. They will also have the opportunity to reflect on and appraise their ability to carry out each step of the interview process and the skills used.

  • Leah Woolner, Rachel Deutsch, Shimmon Hutchinson
  • As an extension to Needs Assessment Throughout the Lifespan I, this course will focus on needs assessment from young adulthood to older adults. Using complex case studies and role-plays, students will be able to complete a thorough needs assessment for an individual seeking help for a given problem. The needs assessment will focus on the individual’s developmental and life cycle stages, social location, individual strengths, and the impact of Social Determinants of Health on needs fulfillment. Students will formulate a comprehensive, non-biased needs assessment. Students will assess resources currently available to the client, including extended family and community support. Based on the needs assessment, they will propose additional interventions and resources and determine where advocacy may be required for the client to access services.

388-2A4-DW
Social Welfare Systems, Legislation and Advocacy
2 sections
  • 00001
  • Cindy Mitchell
  • This course will examine past and current social policy, legislation, and political, social, and economic systems in Quebec and Canada and describe their impacts for individuals, groups, and communities from a structural perspective. The colonial structures on which provincial and federal social welfare systems and policies have been built will be critically analyzed. The course will explore the link between social welfare policy and the social problems of poverty, violence, exclusion, and social inequality. An emphasis on how knowledge about social welfare systems informs social service responses to these social problems, with a focus on human rights, empowerment, advocacy, and activism, will also be examined. Proposed Social Service interventions to address the impact of programs and policies built on dominant social values will be explored using anti-racist, anti-oppressive, intersectional, trauma-informed, Indigenous, and feminist approaches.

388-4A4-DW
Anti-Oppressive Practices with Diverse Communities
2 sections
  • 00001
  • Cindy Mitchell
  • In this course, students will critically assess the systems of oppression (colonialism, racism, ableism, patriarchy, heterosexism, etc.) that pose a threat to universal human rights and create barriers for individuals, groups, and communities in their ability to access resources. Through an anti-oppressive practice lens, students will analyze the adequacy of government programs and policies intended to address problems of poverty, inequality, and exclusion. They will examine actions or acts of resistance by communities, community advocacy groups, and social movements to effect policy change. Relying on research and theory, students will be able to explain the different levels of oppression and how these are perpetuated within various systems (the education and justice systems, health and social services, etc.). Students will then develop an advocacy action plan that could be carried out with members of a given community to address systemic barriers and human rights issues.

388-920-DW
Communication and Wellbeing in the Medical Ultrasound Profession
1 section
  • 00001
  • Felicia D'Orve
  • Through the course Communication and Well-being in the Medical Ultrasound Profession, students will gain knowledge and skills to become effective communicators as future medical ultrasound technologists. The elements of interpersonal communication, the impact of diversity on communication, as well as active listening will be explored, incorporating elements of trauma-informed practice and emphasizing cultural sensitivity and competence. Expressing oneself assertively to meet one's own needs while being “other-oriented” and respecting the needs and rights of others will be practiced. An important part of the course is to develop more awareness of oneself as a communicator, and students will learn to assess their own communication style and the impact of this style on others. Students will learn principles of self and collective care as well as management of professional boundaries to prevent risks of harm and promote ethical practice in the workplace.

Sociology

387-0B2-DW
Social Justice and the Limits of the Law
2 sections
  • 00001
  • Sarah Beer
  • This course examines the dynamic relationship between law and society, focusing on how legal systems shape, and are shaped by, social forces. Through critical sociological theories and case studies, students will explore the definitions and enforcement of law and criminality, as well as the actors and institutions responsible for these processes. Emphasis is placed on understanding how litigation and legal reforms can both advance social justice and expose the limitations of the law in producing equitable change. Students will engage in a major research project, selecting relevant case studies to investigate how law serves as both a tool of social control and a site of resistance. By the end of the course, students will gain an understanding of the law's role in reproducing social inequalities and fostering social change.
  • Law, Society, and Justice

387-A02-DW
Sexuality & Society
3 sections
  • 00001
  • Kelly Phipps
  • Sexuality is an often overlooked but fundamental aspect of the cultural, economic, political, and social organization of society. This course examines the theoretical and methodological approaches used in the sociological study of sexuality. The analysis of sexualities explores sexual practices and behaviours, meanings and identities, power and social control. Throughout the course, students will examine early sex research and the emergence of sexology at the turn of the 20th century, the goals and impacts of liberation movements of the 1960s, and contemporary influences on patterns of sexual identities and behaviours. Students will analyze research, legal cases, and grassroots initiatives to address sexual violence, sex education curricula, use of technology, and social determinants of sexual health, among other topics, by examining the operation of power and social forces in these outcomes.
  • Psychology

387-A03-DW
Sociology of Education
2 sections
  • 00001
  • Elliot Kerr
  • This course is designed to provide students with an exploration of education. We will look at education not only as a system or institution that prepares citizens for the labour force but also look at education as an intensely personal experience that elicits a range of diverse responses from individuals. In this class, we will be looking at different sociological theories that attempt to explain the function of education for society. We will also look at issues of social class, race and gender in schools and to what extent schools reproduce divisions between different groups or help reduce inequalities. We will also look at the culture of schools – Schools provide the backdrop to where much of our personal relationships are formed, we will attempt to try and unpack the culture of schools and how it may lead to the development of our personality.
  • Education, Family, and Childhood

510-213-DW
Drawing 2
2 sections
  • 00001
  • Antoinetta Grassi
  • This Term 2 course continues to focus on drawing from observation, building and expanding upon the technical and interpretive skills acquired in Drawing 1. Subject matter will be varied, from live models, to objects and structures, to interior and exterior spaces. A greater understanding of depth cues through the use of linear perspective, as well as varying line qualities, textures, value relationships and other optical devices, will enable students to create the convincing illusion of volume and depth in their drawings. Students will mediate drawing from observation with an imaginative sensibility. They will experiment with materials and techniques, make sketches and produce large drawings. Students will begin to consider the symbolic and expressive potential of drawing in preparation for a deeper inquiry into the use of metaphor that will be developed further in Drawing 3 (Term 3).

520-903-DW
Renaissance to Baroque Art
1 section
  • 00001
  • David Mitchell
  • This survey of European visual art from the early 14th to the late 18th centuries falls into three divisions: the emergence of painting as a major art form and the rediscovery of the art of classical antiquity in the 1300s and 1400s; the climax of this development in the High Renaissance art of the early 1500s; and the elaboration and transformation of High Renaissance art in the Mannerist art of the later 1500s and the Baroque and neo-Classical art of the 1600s and 1700s. The course builds on the first-term courses in the Bible and Greco-Roman civilization. The artistic upheavals of the Renaissance and Baroque eras are intimately connected with the religious, political, philosophical and scientific upheavals that accompanied them. The aim of this course is to show that, while art exists in its own right, its links to its social and intellectual context are important to an understanding of its meaning and achievement.
